## The idea

This capstone follows one monophonic source far enough to reveal more than a
single phrase. Choose thirty-two to sixty-four bars from the shortlist made in
Lesson 42. The source should contain several phrases, a discernible high point,
some repeated material, and at least one passage that does not yield on the
first hearing or reading. That resistance gives the transcription method real
work to do. Use the four-pass pipeline from
[Lesson 43](../09-transcription/43-four-pass-pipeline.qmd) and the debugging
checks in [Lesson 46](../09-transcription/46-debug-transcription-like-software.qmd)
on a short excerpt before expanding the project.

The completed work has two layers with different responsibilities. A faithful
event list records pitch, absolute start, duration, articulation, dynamics, and
phrase membership as evidence from the source. An expressive renderer decides
how Sonic Pi presents that evidence. Measure or time references and uncertainty
markers remain attached to the events, so any disputed claim can be traced back
to the score page or recording interval that produced it.

Assess the whole candidate before choosing it. Check its widest leap, complete
range, fastest rhythm, accidentals, ornaments, repeated passages, and the
clarity of its source. Four exposed opening bars can lead into a middle section
whose attacks are buried. A less famous but cleanly documented melody often
supports a better capstone because every stage, from transcription to expressive
comparison, remains inspectable.

## Run this

The block models the final representation in two bars. Global starts place
every event on one timeline, while measure and phrase fields preserve useful
review coordinates. The renderer reads articulation and amplitude to shape the
sound without manufacturing a second copy of the notes.

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 74
use_synth :piano

score = [
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :c4, start: 0.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.62, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :d4, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.68, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 1, phrase: :a, note: :e4, start: 2.0, duration: 2.0, amp: 0.78, articulation: :accent},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :g4, start: 4.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.86, articulation: :accent},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :e4, start: 5.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.72, articulation: :detached},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :d4, start: 6.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.66, articulation: :legato},
  {measure: 2, phrase: :a, note: :c4, start: 7.0, duration: 1.0, amp: 0.58, articulation: :legato}
]

define :play_events do |events|
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    release_ratio = event[:articulation] == :detached ? 0.48 : 0.9
    accent_gain = event[:articulation] == :accent ? 0.12 : 0.0
    play event[:note],
      release: event[:duration] * release_ratio,
      amp: event[:amp] + accent_gain
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

play_events score
```

Pitch and amplitude rise together toward G4, marking it in the data as the
intended high point, then both subside toward C. Audition must establish whether
that intention comes across. The detached E shortens only its sounding release.
Its notated duration still occupies a full beat, so the following D arrives at
the same absolute start and the score timeline remains unchanged.

## Change one thing

1. Set every `amp` to 0.7. The melodic contour still reaches G4, but amplitude
   no longer reinforces that high point. Compare the surviving pitch climax
   with the flatter dynamic shape, then decide whether the original values were
   copied from source markings or added by your renderer.
2. Restore the amplitudes and change G's articulation from `:accent` to
   `:legato`. The note remains highest and loudest, though its attack becomes
   less pronounced. This separates structural importance from the emphasis of
   a particular performance.
3. Add `source_time` or `source_page` to every event and a `REVIEW` field to one
   uncertain note. Print those fields before playback. No sound should change;
   the new benefit is a direct path from the event to its evidence.

## Why it works

One event schema allows specialised tools to agree about the same score.
Bar-total checks use starts and durations. Range and leap reports use notes.
The renderer reads articulation and amplitude. Provenance tools read measures
and source locations. Because every tool receives the same shape of data, no
helper needs a private representation for one phrase or exception.

Absolute starts make gaps and overlaps visible without allowing an early error
to shift every later coordinate. Measure numbers preserve the source's own
reference system. Phrase labels add a formal view without splitting events
into duplicated section arrays. When a repeated phrase returns with a variant,
store the new events and label their relationship to the earlier phrase. An
alias would falsely claim that the two passages are identical.

Review should move between scales. Validate every bar first, then loop each
phrase against its source. Step back to compare the full melodic contour and
finally hear the expressive rendering from beginning to end. A local pitch can
be correct while the phrase direction feels wrong; a set of correct phrases
can still produce an unbalanced whole. Each scale reveals a different kind of
error.

Ruby syntax and validation tests can inspect the representation, but they
cannot establish that it matches a recording or that the articulation carries
the intended phrase. Keep the lesson at `draft` until a person has worked
through every requested comparison in Sonic Pi and recorded the remaining
uncertainties honestly.

## Take it further

Complete the thirty-two-to-sixty-four-bar transcription. Include a source
record, bar-by-bar validation report, global range, phrase labels, articulation,
dynamics, and a list of uncertain passages with exact source coordinates. Feed
one score array into two renderers: a strict statement of pitch and time, then
an expressive version. Compare them phrase by phrase and explain every
performance change. Pitch and duration must remain identical between versions,
while the expressive rendering should make high points, repetitions, and
cadences easier to hear.
